subject: ICT450

questions.stem: Nusantara Learning Hub currently keeps student records in separate spreadsheet files. The manager is considering a database management system (DBMS).

subparts.text: Define database, DBMS and database system.
subparts.answer: A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS is software that creates, stores, manages and controls access to a database. A database system is the database, DBMS, application programs, people, procedures and hardware working together.

subparts.text: State FOUR limitations of the file-based approach that a DBMS addresses.
subparts.answer: The limitations include data redundancy, data inconsistency, difficult data sharing, weak concurrency control, limited security, program-data dependence, and difficult backup/recovery.

subparts.text: Explain THREE functions of a DBMS that address those limitations.
subparts.answer: A DBMS provides controlled data sharing, integrity enforcement, security and authorisation, concurrency control, backup and recovery, and a data dictionary.

questions.answer:
a. A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS is software that creates, stores, manages and controls access to a database. A database system is the database, DBMS, application programs, people, procedures and hardware working together.

b. The limitations include data redundancy, data inconsistency, difficult data sharing, weak concurrency control, limited security, program-data dependence, and difficult backup/recovery.

c. A DBMS provides controlled data sharing, integrity enforcement, security and authorisation, concurrency control, backup and recovery, and a data dictionary.

questions.source: ICT200/ICT450 KB Topic 3 Relational Data Model
questions.stem: The relation schema ENROL(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, CourseName, Lecturer, Grade) records student enrolment. Assume StudentID and CourseID together uniquely identify a row.

subparts.text: Identify the primary key and TWO candidate keys.
subparts.answer: Primary key: (StudentID, CourseID). Candidate keys: (StudentID, CourseID); StudentID alone is not a candidate key because a student enrols in many courses, and CourseID alone is not a candidate key because a course has many students.

subparts.text: Explain entity integrity and referential integrity with one example each.
subparts.answer: Entity integrity: a primary-key attribute cannot be null. Referential integrity: a foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value or be null. Example: ENROL.StudentID must exist in STUDENT.StudentID.

subparts.text: Define tuple, attribute, degree and cardinality.
subparts.answer: Tuple = a row; attribute = a column; degree = number of attributes; cardinality = number of tuples.

subparts.text: Explain TWO update anomalies that can occur in this schema.
subparts.answer: StudentName repeats for every enrolment, so a name change may be missed in some rows (update anomaly). Deleting the last enrolment for a course may lose course data (delete anomaly). Inserting a new course before any student enrols is difficult (insert anomaly).

questions.answer:
a. Primary key: (StudentID, CourseID). Candidate keys: (StudentID, CourseID); StudentID alone is not a candidate key because a student enrols in many courses, and CourseID alone is not a candidate key because a course has many students.

b. Entity integrity: a primary-key attribute cannot be null. Referential integrity: a foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value or be null. Example: ENROL.StudentID must exist in STUDENT.StudentID.

c. Tuple = a row; attribute = a column; degree = number of attributes; cardinality = number of tuples.

d. StudentName repeats for every enrolment, so a name change may be missed in some rows (update anomaly). Deleting the last enrolment for a course may lose course data (delete anomaly). Inserting a new course before any student enrols is difficult (insert anomaly).

questions.stem: Cedar Community Library lends books to members. Each book has one publisher; a publisher can publish many books. A member can borrow many books over time, and each loan records the loan date and due date.

subparts.text: Identify the entities, relationships and cardinalities.
subparts.answer: Entities: MEMBER, BOOK, PUBLISHER, LOAN. Relationships: PUBLISHER publishes BOOK (1:M); MEMBER borrows BOOK through LOAN (M:N resolved by LOAN); LOAN has loan date and due date.

subparts.text: Draw an entity-relationship diagram for the scenario.
subparts.answer: A correct ERD shows MEMBER, BOOK, PUBLISHER and LOAN, with 1:M from PUBLISHER to BOOK, 1:M from MEMBER to LOAN, and 1:M from BOOK to LOAN. LOAN is the associative entity for the M:N borrowing relationship.

subparts.text: Map the ERD to a relational schema and mark primary and foreign keys.
subparts.answer: PUBLISHER(PublisherID PK, PublisherName); BOOK(BookID PK, Title, PublisherID FK); MEMBER(MemberID PK, MemberName); LOAN(LoanID PK, MemberID FK, BookID FK, LoanDate, DueDate).

questions.answer:
a. Entities: MEMBER, BOOK, PUBLISHER, LOAN. Relationships: PUBLISHER publishes BOOK (1:M); MEMBER borrows BOOK through LOAN (M:N resolved by LOAN); LOAN has loan date and due date.

b. A correct ERD shows MEMBER, BOOK, PUBLISHER and LOAN, with 1:M from PUBLISHER to BOOK, 1:M from MEMBER to LOAN, and 1:M from BOOK to LOAN. LOAN is the associative entity for the M:N borrowing relationship.

c. PUBLISHER(PublisherID PK, PublisherName); BOOK(BookID PK, Title, PublisherID FK); MEMBER(MemberID PK, MemberName); LOAN(LoanID PK, MemberID FK, BookID FK, LoanDate, DueDate).

questions.stem: The relation ORDER(OrderID, CustomerID, CustomerName, ProductID, ProductName, Quantity, UnitPrice) has these functional dependencies: OrderID → CustomerID, CustomerName; CustomerID → CustomerName; ProductID → ProductName; (OrderID, ProductID) → Quantity, UnitPrice.

subparts.text: Identify the candidate key and all functional dependencies.
subparts.answer: Candidate key: (OrderID, ProductID). FDs: OrderID → CustomerID, CustomerName; CustomerID → CustomerName; ProductID → ProductName; (OrderID, ProductID) → Quantity, UnitPrice.

1NF: all attributes are atomic. 2NF: 1NF and every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole candidate key. 3NF: 2NF and no non-key attribute is transitively dependent on the key.

subparts.text: Identify the partial and transitive dependencies.
subparts.answer: Partial: OrderID → CustomerID/CustomerName and ProductID → ProductName depend on part of the key. Transitive: OrderID → CustomerID → CustomerName.

CUSTOMER(CustomerID PK, CustomerName); PRODUCT(ProductID PK, ProductName); ORDER_HEADER(OrderID PK, CustomerID FK); ORDER_LINE(OrderID PK, ProductID PK, Quantity, UnitPrice, FKs to ORDER_HEADER and PRODUCT).

questions.answer:
a. Candidate key: (OrderID, ProductID). FDs: OrderID → CustomerID, CustomerName; CustomerID → CustomerName; ProductID → ProductName; (OrderID, ProductID) → Quantity, UnitPrice.

b. 1NF: all attributes are atomic. 2NF: 1NF and every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole candidate key. 3NF: 2NF and no non-key attribute is transitively dependent on the key.

c. Partial: OrderID → CustomerID/CustomerName and ProductID → ProductName depend on part of the key. Transitive: OrderID → CustomerID → CustomerName.

d. CUSTOMER(CustomerID PK, CustomerName); PRODUCT(ProductID PK, ProductName); ORDER_HEADER(OrderID PK, CustomerID FK); ORDER_LINE(OrderID PK, ProductID PK, Quantity, UnitPrice, FKs to ORDER_HEADER and PRODUCT).

questions.stem: Sri Murni Health Clinic is planning a database for patients, doctors, appointments and prescriptions. The project will follow the database life cycle.

subparts.text: List FOUR phases of the database life cycle and state one activity in each.
subparts.answer: Database initial study, database design, implementation and loading, testing and evaluation, operation, maintenance and evolution. Activities include requirements analysis, conceptual/logical design, creating storage structures, loading data, testing, and tuning.

subparts.text: Differentiate the SDLC and the DBLC.
subparts.answer: SDLC covers the whole information-system life cycle; DBLC focuses on the database component within that system and runs through its own design, implementation, testing, operation and maintenance phases.

subparts.text: Compare top-down and bottom-up database design.
subparts.answer: Top-down starts from the overall data model and breaks it into components. Bottom-up starts from individual data elements and combines them into a model.
Centralized design is controlled by one design team or location. Decentralized design distributes design work across teams or locations and requires reconciliation.

questions.answer:
a. Database initial study, database design, implementation and loading, testing and evaluation, operation, maintenance and evolution. Activities include requirements analysis, conceptual/logical design, creating storage structures, loading data, testing, and tuning.

b. SDLC covers the whole information-system life cycle; DBLC focuses on the database component within that system and runs through its own design, implementation, testing, operation and maintenance phases.

c. Top-down starts from the overall data model and breaks it into components. Bottom-up starts from individual data elements and combines them into a model.

d. Centralized design is controlled by one design team or location. Decentralized design distributes design work across teams or locations and requires reconciliation.
